title: Paul Buchheit: Why "bad" product ideas are often the best ones
summary: Paul Buchheit splits product ideas into three types and argues the real low-hanging fruit sits in the "bad ideas" category, because good and bad ideas are nearly indistinguishable up front. His takeaways: test ideas faster and cheaper instead of debating them, and remember an idea is worthless until you build a real product.

principles.text: The best product ideas are often found in the "bad ideas" category, so expect skeptics and build anyway.
principles.quote: The best product ideas are often found in the "bad ideas" category!

principles.text: People can't reliably tell good ideas from bad ones in advance; even the best pickers are right about half the time.
principles.quote: Everyone thinks that they can tell which ideas are the good ones, but observation suggests that they can't. I do believe that some people are better at picking winners than others, but at best they have maybe 50% accuracy.

principles.text: Stop debating whether an idea is good; build faster, cheaper ways to test it.
principles.quote: Instead of endlessly debating whether an idea is good or not, we should find faster and cheaper ways of testing them.

principles.text: Open systems where small groups can build without approval move faster than closed ones or big companies.
principles.quote: individuals and small groups are able to build new things without getting approval from anyone.

principles.text: An idea alone is worthless; shipping a real product proves it isn't bad and proves you can execute.
principles.quote: The way to make your idea valuable is to demonstrate that it's not bad by building a real product -- this also demonstrates your ability to execute.

principles.text: Negative expectations and a bad first experience can sink a good idea; Google Video's clunky upload let YouTube win.
principles.quote: Unfortunately Google Video was burdened with an incredibly bad upload process (it included installing a windows client to do the upload!), and YouTube, which was started AFTER Google Video launched, took over.
